title: Curved manifolds
one_line_summary: Builds the geometry of curved spacetime: manifolds and tensors, the metric and the local-flatness theorem (with a counting proof that 20 second derivatives of the metric carry the curvature), covariant derivatives defined through local inertial frames, proper volume and Gauss's law, parallel transport and geodesics, the Riemann tensor from transport round a tiny loop, geodesic deviation, and the Bianchi identities that make the Einstein tensor divergence-free.
role_in_book: This is the mathematical core of Schutz's route to general relativity. Chapter 5 argued physically that gravity rules out global inertial frames and rehearsed curvilinear calculus in the flat plane; Chapter 6 transplants that calculus to an arbitrary (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold, using the local inertial frame as the bridge that turns flat-space formulas into general tensor equations. It hands Chapter 7 the tools for doing physics in curved spacetime (covariant derivative, geodesic equation, proper volume, divergence formula) and hands Chapter 8 the curvature machinery (Riemann, Ricci and Einstein tensors plus the Bianchi identities) from which the field equations G = 8 pi T and automatic energy-momentum conservation follow. Later chapters on stars, black holes and cosmology reuse its exercises' metrics (static spherical line element, three-sphere).

assumed_background.topic: One-forms, gradients, tensors as linear machines, the (M N) type classification and index raising with a metric
Gauss's law (divergence theorem) for four-dimensional regions in special relativity
Physical argument that gravity allows only local inertial frames; equivalence principle
Curvilinear coordinates, Jacobians, Christoffel symbols and the covariant derivative in the flat plane, including the formula for Gamma in terms of metric derivatives
Noncoordinate bases and the integrability condition for a basis to come from coordinates
Multivariable Taylor expansion, change of variables in multiple integrals, symmetry of mixed partial derivatives
Determinants, transposes, eigenvalues and diagonalization of real symmetric matrices
Euler-Lagrange equations for an extremal of an integral
Great circles, spherical triangles and spherical polar coordinates
Elementary topology (torus versus plane, local versus global properties)

learning_objectives: Reader can explain what makes a set a manifold (smooth local labelling by n numbers) and give examples, including the three-dimensional manifold of rotations and a torus whose global topology differs from the plane.
Reader can separate what differentiability alone provides (vectors, one-forms, all tensor types) from what a metric adds (lengths, volumes, index raising, curvature).
Reader can state the local-flatness theorem (metric equals eta and its first derivatives vanish at a chosen point) and explain why a pointwise orthonormal basis need not come from coordinates.
Reader can reproduce the Taylor-coefficient counting argument (16 vs 10, 40 vs 40, 80 vs 100) and interpret the leftover 6 Lorentz freedoms and 20 curvature quantities.
Reader can compute the proper length of a curve and the proper volume element sqrt(-g) d^4x, including the determinant trick that avoids computing a Jacobian directly.
Reader can justify metric compatibility g_{alpha beta;gamma} = 0 from a local inertial frame and derive the Christoffel-symbol formula from it.
Reader can use V^alpha_{;alpha} = (sqrt(-g) V^alpha)_{,alpha}/sqrt(-g) and state Gauss's law on a curved manifold with proper volume and surface elements.
Reader can distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic curvature using the cylinder and sphere, and demonstrate path dependence of parallel transport with the octant triangle.
Reader can write the parallel-transport and geodesic equations, explain affine parameters and why only linear reparametrizations preserve the geodesic equation.
Reader can derive the Riemann tensor from parallel transport around an infinitesimal coordinate loop and say what each index slot does.
Reader can express Riemann in a local inertial frame through second metric derivatives, list its symmetries and cyclic identity, and count 20 independent components in four dimensions.
Reader can show that the commutator of covariant derivatives is given by the Riemann tensor, and relate this to loop transport.
Reader can derive the geodesic deviation equation and interpret it as the geometric description of tidal forces.

Reader can derive the Bianchi identities, define the Ricci tensor, Ricci scalar and Einstein tensor, and show that the Einstein tensor is divergence-free, anticipating conservation of T in Einstein's equations.

teaching_approach.summary: A chapter in which local flatness does nearly all the work. Almost every result is first obtained at a single point in locally inertial coordinates, where Christoffel symbols vanish and formulas collapse to flat-space or partial-derivative forms, and is then promoted to every coordinate system because it is a tensor equation. Curvature is motivated by low-tech pictures on a sphere (meridians meeting at the pole, a vector drawn by a two-dimensional ant that comes back turned by a right angle) before being formalized with integrals round a tiny coordinate cell. Counting arguments (free Taylor coefficients against constraints) supply intuition for why curvature lives in second derivatives before the Riemann tensor exists. Physical meaning (rods and clocks, free particles, tidal forces, the future field equations) is kept in view, but the chapter is openly mathematical, hands many algebraic steps to exercises, and closes by urging understanding of derivations over memorization.
narrative_arc: Define a manifold as anything that can be smoothly parametrized, note that differentiability alone yields vectors, one-forms and tensors, and review the permissible tensor operations and the rule that a tensor equation valid in one basis is valid in all.

Add a metric as extra structure, bring it to diag(-1,1,1,1) at a point by a matrix theorem, identify signature +2 with the physical existence of local inertial frames, and warn that the pointwise diagonalizing basis is generally not a coordinate basis.
State the local-flatness theorem and put it straight to work: proper length of curves and the proper volume element sqrt(-g) d^4x via a determinant identity, checked on spherical coordinates.
Prove local flatness by counting Taylor coefficients, finding that exactly 20 second derivatives of the metric resist removal: a preview of the curvature tensor.

Define the covariant derivative as the ordinary derivative in a local inertial frame, deduce metric compatibility and the Christoffel formula for any metric, and derive the compact divergence formula and Gauss's law.

Distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic curvature (paper rolled into a cylinder versus the sphere) and exhibit intrinsic curvature with converging meridians and a vector rotated 90 degrees by parallel transport round a spherical triangle.
Formalize parallel transport and geodesics (straight lines reinterpreted as curves transporting their own tangent), discuss affine parameters and the extremal-length property.

Define the Riemann tensor by transporting a vector around an infinitesimal coordinate loop, evaluate it in a local inertial frame, extract its symmetries and 20 components, and equate its vanishing with flatness.
Show that Riemann is the commutator of covariant derivatives and derive geodesic deviation, identifying curvature with tidal forces.

Differentiate Riemann to get the Bianchi identities, contract to the Ricci tensor and scalar, construct the identically divergence-free Einstein tensor, and preview G = 8 pi T with conservation of stress-energy.
Close with a numbered perspective list of the essential facts and an explicit statement that geometric understanding matters more than memorizing formulas.
signature_moves: Local-inertial-frame promotion: compute at one point where Gamma = 0 (but its derivatives do not vanish), then declare the result a tensor equation valid everywhere; used for metric compatibility, parallel transport, the commutator identity, geodesic deviation and the Bianchi identities.

Degrees-of-freedom bookkeeping: compare freely choosable Taylor coefficients of a coordinate change (16, 40, 80) with metric data (10, 40, 100) to prove local flatness and predict 20 curvature components before defining the Riemann tensor, then close the loop when the Riemann symmetries also give 20.
Determinant shortcut for the Jacobian: det g = -(det Lambda)^2 so the volume factor is sqrt(-g), avoiding a 4x4 determinant of partial derivatives.
Sphere pictures before formulas: meridians meeting at the pole and a vector drawn by a 2D ant around an octant triangle establish curvature as path dependence of parallelism.
Rereading Euclid: extending a straight line means keeping its direction, which becomes the definition of a geodesic as a curve that parallel-transports its own tangent.
Tensor-as-machine reading of Riemann: its four slots take a basis one-form, the transported vector, and the two edge vectors of the loop, and the output is the component of the change in the vector.
Identity-first view of curvature: the Bianchi identities and the Einstein tensor are derived as pure geometry, with the physical payoff (G = 8 pi T implies local conservation) only previewed.
Derivation steps are routinely delegated to 'fill in the algebra' exercises, so the exercise set is part of the exposition.

sections.title: Differentiable manifolds and tensors
sections.summary: Introduces a manifold as a set that can be continuously labelled by a fixed number of parameters and that looks Euclidean in small patches while possibly having a different global topology (sphere, flat hyperplanes, rotations via Euler angles, torus). Restricts attention to differentiable manifolds (a cone fails at its apex) and observes that differentiability already supplies gradient one-forms, tangent vectors defined as derivatives along curves, and the full family of tensors, but no correspondence between vectors and one-forms because there is no metric yet. Ends with a numbered review of tensor algebra culminating in the principle that a tensor equation true in one basis is true in every basis.
concepts: tangent vector as derivative along a curve
key_moves: Characterize a manifold by continuous parametrization; the dimension is the number of parameters.
Use the rotation group to show points of a manifold need not be places in physical space.
Separate local Euclidean behaviour from global topology with the torus.
Define a tangent vector as the linear map taking d-tilde-phi to d phi / d lambda (Eq. 6.1), using only differentiability.
List permissible tensor operations and derive the one-basis-implies-all-bases rule that powers the rest of the chapter.

sections.title: Riemannian manifolds
sections.summary: Adds a metric as a chosen symmetric (0 2) tensor field, stressing that it is extra structure which fixes distances and curvature (the same manifold could be a sphere or an ellipsoid); the book uses 'Riemannian' for indefinite metrics too and mentions affine manifolds only in passing. The metric raises and lowers indices, and all nonsingular coordinate transformations must now be allowed. A matrix theorem brings the metric to diag(-1,1,1,1) at a point; signature +2 is tied to the physical existence of local inertial frames, while the pointwise diagonalizing basis is generally not a coordinate basis. The local-flatness theorem is then stated (Eqs. 6.3-6.5): coordinates exist with g = eta and vanishing first derivatives at P, but second derivatives generally survive, and free particles move on locally straight lines in such coordinates.
concepts: canonical form of the metric at a point
key_moves: Treat the metric as structure added to a bare differentiable manifold.
Diagonalize the metric at one point to +/-1 entries and read off the signature.
Link signature +2 to the equivalence-principle requirement of a local inertial frame at every event.
Use the Chapter 5 integrability condition to show pointwise orthonormal bases do not generally integrate to global Lorentz coordinates.
State local flatness to first order and flag nonvanishing second derivatives as the signature of curvature.

sections.title: Lengths and volumes (within 6.2)
sections.summary: Uses the line element to define the length of an arbitrary curve as the integral of |V.V|^{1/2} along its parameter. For four-volumes, argues that d^4x in a local inertial frame is the physically measured volume, then transforms to arbitrary coordinates: writing the metric transformation as a matrix product and taking determinants gives det g = -(det Lambda)^2, so the Jacobian is sqrt(-g) and the proper volume element is sqrt(-g) d^4x. The authors highlight this as the prototype of a recurring argument, and check the positive-definite analogue on three-dimensional spherical coordinates, recovering r^2 sin theta dr dtheta dphi.
key_moves: Write length as an integral of the square root of |g_{alpha beta} dx^alpha dx^beta| and re-express with the tangent vector (Eq. 6.8).
Identify the local-inertial-frame coordinate volume with the rods-and-clocks volume.
Take determinants of (g) = (Lambda)(eta)(Lambda)^T to get the Jacobian from the metric (Eqs. 6.11-6.17).
Verify with the spherical-coordinate metric diag(1, r^2, r^2 sin^2 theta).

sections.title: Local flatness and curvature: proof by counting (within 6.2)
sections.summary: Proves the local-flatness theorem by expanding both the transformation matrix and the metric in Taylor series about P and substituting into the tensor transformation law. At each order the number of freely choosable derivatives of the coordinate transformation is compared with the number of metric quantities to be fixed: 16 entries of Lambda can satisfy the 10 conditions g = eta, leaving 6 that are exactly the boosts and rotations; 40 second derivatives of the transformation just suffice to kill the 40 first derivatives of g; but only 80 third derivatives are available against 100 second derivatives of g. The 20 left over are real geometric information, later identified with the independent components of the curvature tensor.
concepts: curvature as irreducible second derivatives of the metric
key_moves: Taylor-expand x^alpha(x') and g_{alpha beta} about P (Eqs. 6.23-6.26).
Count symmetric index combinations: 4x10 = 40, 4x20 = 80, 10x10 = 100, using n(n+1)(n+2)/3! for three symmetric indices.
Match unknowns to equations order by order and interpret the surplus (6) and deficit (20).
Conclude that a metric is characterized at a point by its 20 irreducible second derivatives.

sections.title: Covariant differentiation on a general manifold
sections.summary: Faces the problem that comparing vectors at separated points is ambiguous in curved space and resolves it by definition: at P, the basis vectors of a local inertial frame are declared to have zero derivative, so covariant derivatives reduce to partial derivatives there and Christoffel symbols vanish. Applying this to the metric gives g_{alpha beta;gamma} = 0 at P, and because this is a tensor equation it holds everywhere; with symmetric Christoffel symbols (Exercise 6.5) the flat-space derivation of Gamma in terms of metric derivatives carries over to any metric. Emphasizes that Gamma can vanish at a point but not in a neighbourhood, so curvature shows up in derivatives of Gamma. Recaps covariant derivatives of vectors, one-forms and (2 0) tensors.
concepts: covariant derivative on a curved manifold
key_moves: Explicitly adopt, as a definition justified by physics, that local-inertial basis vectors are constant at P.
Show nabla g = 0 in one frame, then everywhere.
Reuse Chapter 5's algebra to get Gamma from the metric for any geometry.
Contrast flat space (Gamma = 0 everywhere in suitable coordinates) with curved space (Gamma = 0 only at a point).

sections.title: Divergence and Gauss' law (within 6.3)
sections.summary: Simplifies the contracted Christoffel symbol by noting that an antisymmetric bracket contracted with the symmetric inverse metric vanishes, and uses the derivative of the determinant to write Gamma^alpha_{mu alpha} as the logarithmic derivative of sqrt(-g). This turns the divergence into (sqrt(-g) V^alpha)_{,alpha}/sqrt(-g), an ordinary divergence to which the special-relativistic Gauss theorem applies, yielding Gauss's law on a curved manifold with the proper volume element and proper surface element.
concepts: Gauss's law on a curved manifold
key_moves: Split Gamma^alpha_{mu alpha} into an antisymmetric part that cancels and (1/2) g^{alpha beta} g_{alpha beta, mu}.
Use g_{,mu} = g g^{alpha beta} g_{beta alpha, mu} (Exercise 6.7).
Rewrite the divergence as a total derivative and invoke the flat Gauss theorem.

sections.title: Parallel transport, geodesics, and curvature
sections.summary: Distinguishes extrinsic curvature (bending relative to an enclosing space) from intrinsic curvature (detectable from within); a cylinder rolled from paper is intrinsically flat, and GR's spacetime curvature is intrinsic because world lines never leave spacetime. The sphere's intrinsic curvature is shown twice: two meridians leaving the equator parallel meet at the pole, and a vector carried parallel to itself around a triangle with two corners on the equator and one at the pole comes back rotated by 90 degrees, whereas the same construction in flat space returns the vector unchanged. Hence parallelism is path dependent and there are no globally parallel fields. Parallel transport is formalized as U^beta V^alpha_{;beta} = 0; geodesics are curves that transport their own tangent, obeying a second-order ODE with unique solutions for given position and direction; affine parameters are defined up to linear change; geodesics extremize length, and proper length is affine (exercises).
concepts: failure of parallelism on a sphere
key_moves: Cylinder from rolled paper: all Euclid's axioms hold, only topology is odd.
Meridians perpendicular to the equator converge at the pole.
Step-by-step transport around the octant triangle produces a quarter-turn.
Constant components in a local inertial frame become the covariant statement nabla_U V = 0 (Eqs. 6.46-6.48).
Euclid's 'extend a line' reinterpreted as transporting the tangent: nabla_U U = 0 and the geodesic equation (Eq. 6.51).
Show linear reparametrizations preserve the geodesic equation; nonlinear ones do not.

sections.title: The curvature tensor
sections.summary: Makes the sphere's loop discrepancy quantitative. A vector is transported around a tiny loop bounded by coordinate lines; the four edge integrals would cancel pairwise if Gamma and V were constant, so to first order in the cell size the net change is delta a delta b times derivatives of Gamma V across the cell, and eliminating derivatives of V gives an expression linear in V, antisymmetric in the two loop directions, and linear in the loop edges. This defines the (1 3) Riemann tensor (Eq. 6.63), valid only for loops small compared with the curvature scale. In a local inertial frame Riemann becomes a combination of second metric derivatives (Eq. 6.68), from which its antisymmetries, pair symmetry and cyclic identity follow; these leave 20 independent components in four dimensions, matching the counting proof, and flatness is equivalent to R = 0. A footnote warns that sign and index conventions differ between texts.
concepts: Riemann tensor in a local inertial frame
key_moves: Integrate the transport law along each of four coordinate edges (Eqs. 6.53-6.57).
Pair opposite edges and expand the difference to first order in the cell size (Eqs. 6.58-6.60).
Eliminate derivatives of V with the transport law and relabel dummy indices (Eq. 6.61).
Argue tensor character from linearity in the one-form, the vector and both edge vectors (Eqs. 6.62-6.63).
Evaluate at the origin of local inertial coordinates to express R through second derivatives of g and read off symmetries (Eqs. 6.64-6.70).

sections.title: Covariant derivatives do not commute; geodesic deviation (within 6.5)
sections.summary: Computes two successive covariant derivatives of a vector in local inertial coordinates, where Gamma vanishes but its derivatives do not; subtracting the reversed order cancels the symmetric second partial derivatives and leaves derivatives of Gamma, which match the Riemann tensor, giving [nabla_alpha, nabla_beta] V^mu = R^mu_{nu alpha beta} V^nu in any basis, with one Riemann term per index for higher-rank tensors. This is linked back to loop transport. Geodesic deviation is then derived: the connecting vector between equal-parameter points on two initially parallel geodesics obeys nabla_V nabla_V xi^alpha = R^alpha_{mu nu beta} V^mu V^nu xi^beta, the geometric expression of tidal forces.
key_moves: Second covariant derivative in local inertial coordinates keeps a Gamma_{,alpha} V term (Eq. 6.73).
Antisymmetrize; partial derivatives of V commute and drop out (Eqs. 6.75-6.76).
Identify the remainder with Riemann and promote (Eq. 6.77).
Write geodesic equations at A and A', Taylor-expand Gamma at A' in xi, subtract (Eqs. 6.79-6.83).
Convert d^2 xi/d lambda^2 to a second covariant derivative using initial parallelism, and recognize R^alpha_{00 beta} (Eqs. 6.84-6.87).

sections.title: Bianchi identities; Ricci and Einstein tensors
sections.summary: Differentiates the local-inertial-frame form of Riemann once more; the cyclic sum over the derivative index and the last two indices vanishes by symmetry of partial derivatives, and since Gamma = 0 at the point the commas may be replaced by semicolons, giving the Bianchi identities as tensor equations. Defines the Ricci tensor as the contraction on first and third indices (essentially the only independent contraction, and symmetric) and the Ricci scalar. Contracting the Bianchi identities twice, with metric compatibility letting g pass through covariant derivatives and antisymmetry fixing signs, yields (2R^mu_lambda - delta^mu_lambda R)_{;mu} = 0, i.e. the Einstein tensor G = Ric - (1/2) g R is identically divergence-free. Previews G = 8 pi T and the resulting conservation of stress-energy.
key_moves: Differentiate Eq. 6.68 and form the cyclic sum (Eqs. 6.88-6.89).
Replace partial by covariant derivatives at the point where Gamma = 0 (Eq. 6.90).
Contract with g^{alpha mu} using nabla g = 0 and antisymmetry (Eqs. 6.93-6.95).
Contract again with g^{beta nu} to reach the twice-contracted identity (Eqs. 6.96-6.97).
Package the result as G^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 (Eqs. 6.98-6.99) and preview the field equations.

sections.title: Curvature in perspective
sections.summary: A six-point recap: work on smooth manifolds with a metric of signature +2; at any point coordinates exist with g = eta and vanishing first derivatives (so Gamma = 0 there); the proper volume element is |g|^{1/2} d^4x; covariant differentiation is ordinary differentiation in local inertial coordinates and fails to commute because derivatives of Gamma do not vanish; parallel transport means zero covariant derivative along a curve and geodesics transport their own tangent with proper distance as affine parameter; the Riemann tensor fully characterizes curvature, has 20 components, obeys the Bianchi identities and depends on g and its first two derivatives, while Ricci, Ricci scalar and the ten-component Einstein tensor are contractions satisfying four differential identities. The authors say derivations and geometric meaning matter more than memorized formulas.
concepts: covariant derivative on a curved manifold
key_moves: Compress the chapter into an ordered list of structural facts.
Count Einstein tensor components (10) against differential identities (4).
Set expectations: interpretation will be built over coming chapters.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Points to further reading on differentiable manifolds with a physics slant (Abraham et al., Bishop and Goldberg, Lovelock and Rund, Schutz's own geometrical-methods book), to classic mathematical references (Kobayashi and Nomizu, Schouten, Spivak), to Needham's almost algebra-free visual differential geometry, and to Nahmad-Achar for topology applied to relativity.
key_moves: Separate physics-oriented, rigorous-mathematics and visual-geometry routes for further study.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Thirty-nine exercises. Many complete derivations from the text (component counts, symmetry of Gamma, determinant derivative, loop algebra, Riemann symmetries, commutator, geodesic deviation, Bianchi contractions). Others compute: Riemann for polar coordinates of the plane, the unit sphere and the cylinder; the metric of spheres and the three-sphere with proper areas and lengths; 20 Riemann components of a static spherically symmetric metric; a local inertial frame for a weak-field metric and its acceleration. Conceptual problems cover what counts as a manifold, angular excess versus transport rotation, integrability of globally parallel fields, preservation of inner products under transport, and the Lie bracket and Lie derivative.
key_moves: Complete the chapter's derivations as graded exercises.
Compute curvature for flat-but-curvilinear, cylindrical and spherical geometries to calibrate intuition.
Introduce the Lie derivative as a connection-free derivative.

concepts.name: manifold
concepts.definition: A set of points that, near every point, can be labelled continuously and one-to-one by n real numbers (coordinates), so that small patches correspond to regions of n-dimensional Euclidean space; n is the dimension, and the large-scale shape or topology may differ from Euclidean space.
concepts.how_introduced: Opened with examples of rising abstraction (the sphere with theta and phi, flat m-dimensional hyperplanes, the set of rigid rotations labelled by Euler angles); the key idea is continuous parametrization pictured as a map from points to n-tuples, with the torus showing that only the local correspondence is required.
concepts.notes: Schutz calls it a formal word for 'space'; charts, atlases and overlap maps are not discussed.

concepts.name: manifold of rotations
concepts.definition: All possible rigid rotations of a Cartesian frame in ordinary 3D space, regarded as one space: each rotation is a point, labelled by two angles giving the axis and one giving the turn (equivalently three Euler angles), so the collection is a three-dimensional manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the abstract example proving that points of a manifold need not be locations in physical space.
concepts.notes: Its global topology is not that of ordinary 3D space, a subtlety the chapter does not pursue.

concepts.name: global topology versus local structure
concepts.definition: A manifold is required to resemble Euclidean space only in small neighbourhoods; its global connectivity can differ, as for a torus, or a cylinder on which a straight path returns to its starting point.
concepts.how_introduced: The torus is contrasted with the plane in 6.1; the cylinder in 6.4 is intrinsically flat yet topologically unusual.

concepts.name: differentiable manifold
concepts.definition: A manifold for which, around each point, a smooth map to Euclidean space exists that allows derivatives of scalar functions to be defined; it may fail at isolated points such as the apex of a cone. Its 'differential structure' includes all vector, one-form and tensor fields, which need no metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the only kind used in the book, with the sphere (smooth everywhere) and cone (singular at its tip) as examples; spacetimes of GR are asserted to be differentiable.

concepts.name: tangent vector as derivative along a curve
concepts.definition: For a curve with parameter lambda, the tangent vector is the linear map that sends the gradient one-form of any scalar phi to d phi/d lambda along the curve; its coordinate components are dx^alpha/d lambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in one line (Eq. 6.1) from differentiability alone, reusing the one-form picture of Chapter 3.

concepts.name: gradient one-form
concepts.definition: The one-form field whose components in any coordinates are the partial derivatives of a scalar field; combinations of such gradients with function coefficients are also one-form fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the start of 6.1 as something any differentiable manifold possesses without a metric.

concepts.name: permissible tensor operations
concepts.definition: Operations on tensor components guaranteed to give components of another tensor: multiplication by a scalar field, addition of same-type tensors, outer product, covariant differentiation (adds one lower index), and contraction of one upper with one lower index.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a numbered review list in 6.1 to make type-checking of later derivations routine.

concepts.name: basis independence of tensor equations
aliases: true in one basis, true in all
concepts.definition: An equation assembled only from tensor components with permissible operations, if valid in one basis, is valid in every basis, because it states equality of two tensors of the same type.
concepts.how_introduced: Rule (6) of the 6.1 review; it becomes the engine of the chapter, letting results computed in local inertial frames be generalized.
concepts.notes: Equations containing bare partial derivatives or Christoffel symbols (e.g. 6.67, 6.73) are frame-specific and cannot be promoted.

concepts.name: metric tensor
concepts.definition: A symmetric, invertible (0 2) tensor field g that assigns inner products to pairs of vectors at each point, thereby fixing lengths, proper times, angles and the vector/one-form correspondence; its components are g_{alpha beta} with inverse g^{alpha beta}.
concepts.how_introduced: Reintroduced from special relativity as what carries clock rates and distances; now a position-dependent field.

concepts.name: Riemannian manifold
concepts.definition: A differentiable manifold with a metric tensor field specified at every point. Strictly the term requires a positive-definite metric and an indefinite one (as in SR and GR) makes the manifold pseudo-Riemannian, but the book deliberately uses one name for both.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the physical need for distances and clock rates; the positive-definite subtlety is noted and set aside.

concepts.name: metric as added structure
aliases: choice of metric fixes the shape
concepts.definition: A bare differentiable manifold has no notion of distance or shape; choosing a metric adds that structure, and different metrics on the same manifold (for example round sphere versus ellipsoid of revolution) give different curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with the 'amorphous' differentiable manifold at the start of 6.2.

concepts.name: affine connection without metric
concepts.definition: A rule for covariant differentiation and parallel transport given independently of any metric; it already defines curvature, and some texts develop geometry this way.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only for completeness and then set aside because GR's curvature comes from the metric.

concepts.name: raising and lowering indices
concepts.definition: Using g_{alpha beta} and its inverse to convert between vector and one-form components, V_alpha = g_{alpha beta} V^beta and back; with position-dependent metric components the relation between, say, V_0 and V^0 is no longer a simple sign change.
concepts.how_introduced: Restated from SR with the warning that general coordinates make it nontrivial.

concepts.name: general coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: Any smooth relabelling of points whose matrix Lambda^{alpha'}_beta = dx^{alpha'}/dx^beta is invertible; in curved spacetime all such transformations must be admitted because gravity prevents a global Lorentz frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the physics of Chapter 5; nonsingularity as defined in 5.2.

concepts.name: canonical form of the metric at a point
concepts.definition: At a single point, a suitable change of basis turns any real symmetric metric matrix into a diagonal matrix with entries +1, -1 or 0, where the numbers of +1 and -1 entries equal the numbers of positive and negative eigenvalues and are basis-independent; for an invertible metric no zeros occur.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as a well-known matrix theorem (proof sketched in Exercise 6.3) and applied to a metric with three positive and one negative eigenvalue to obtain eta.
concepts.notes: The name Sylvester is not used in the book.

concepts.name: metric signature
concepts.definition: The sum of the diagonal entries of the metric in its canonical +/-1 form; with one timelike and three spacelike directions and Schutz's (-,+,+,+) sign choice it equals +2.
concepts.how_introduced: Tied to physics: local inertial frames must exist at every event, so the metric must reduce to eta, which forces signature +2.
prerequisites: canonical form of the metric at a point

concepts.name: noncoordinate basis
concepts.definition: A field of basis vectors or one-forms not generated by any coordinate system; one-forms Lambda^{alpha'}_beta dx^beta come from coordinates only if the derivative of Lambda in one index is symmetric with another index (the Chapter 5 integrability condition).
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why diagonalizing the metric point by point does not produce global Lorentz coordinates in a gravitational field.

concepts.name: local flatness theorem
concepts.definition: About any point P of a (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold there exist coordinates with origin at P in which g_{alpha beta}(P) = eta_{alpha beta} and every first partial derivative of g_{alpha beta} vanishes at P; some second derivatives remain nonzero unless the manifold is flat.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated early (Eqs. 6.3-6.5) as the mathematical version of freely falling frames and immediately used; proved at the end of 6.2 by counting Taylor coefficients.
prerequisites: canonical form of the metric at a point
concepts.notes: Geometric form of the equivalence principle; the intuitive gloss is that every curved space has a flat tangent space at each point.

concepts.name: local inertial frame
concepts.definition: Coordinates satisfying the local-flatness conditions at a point: the metric is Minkowskian there with corrections of second order in coordinate distance, Christoffel symbols vanish at the point, and free particles move on locally straight lines.
concepts.how_introduced: Named right after Eq. 6.3 and identified with the freely falling frames of Chapter 5; used throughout as the computational setting for every derivation.
concepts.notes: Riemann normal coordinates are a standard refinement; that name is not used here.

concepts.name: coefficient counting argument
concepts.definition: Deciding what a coordinate change can remove at a point by comparing its freely choosable Taylor coefficients (16 first derivatives, 40 second, 80 third) with the metric data at each order (10 values, 40 first derivatives, 100 second derivatives).
concepts.how_introduced: Serves as the proof of local flatness: the surplus at zeroth order is 6, the first-order match is exact, and 20 second-derivative combinations cannot be removed.
concepts.notes: A plausibility count assuming generic independence of the equations rather than a rigorous existence proof.

concepts.name: residual Lorentz freedom
aliases: six-parameter freedom of a local inertial frame
concepts.definition: After the ten conditions g = eta at P are imposed on the sixteen entries of the transformation matrix, six remain free; they are the three boosts and three rotations preserving eta, so a local inertial frame is unique only up to a Lorentz transformation.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off as the leftover from the zeroth-order count.

concepts.name: curvature as irreducible second derivatives of the metric
concepts.definition: At a point, the metric value and its first derivatives carry no coordinate-invariant information, since they can be set to eta and zero; genuine geometry resides in the 20 combinations of second derivatives that no coordinate change removes.
concepts.how_introduced: Conclusion of the counting proof, later matched to the 20 independent components of the Riemann tensor.

concepts.name: line element
concepts.definition: The quadratic form g_{alpha beta} dx^alpha dx^beta giving the squared length (or interval) of an infinitesimal displacement.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the starting point for curve lengths.

concepts.name: proper length of a curve
concepts.definition: The integral along a parametrized curve of the square root of |g_{alpha beta} (dx^alpha/d lambda)(dx^beta/d lambda)|, equivalently of |V.V|^{1/2} d lambda with V the tangent; it does not depend on the choice of parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the line element, then rewritten with the tangent vector (Eqs. 6.6-6.8).
prerequisites: tangent vector as derivative along a curve

concepts.name: Jacobian determinant
concepts.definition: The determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives relating two coordinate systems, which is the factor converting one coordinate volume element into the other.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from multivariable calculus and 5.2 as the formal but tedious route to the volume element.

concepts.name: metric determinant
concepts.definition: The determinant g of the matrix of metric components in given coordinates; negative for a Lorentzian metric, equal to -(Jacobian)^2 relative to a local inertial frame, and with derivative g_{,mu} = g g^{alpha beta} g_{beta alpha,mu}.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the shortcut to the Jacobian via determinants of the matrix transformation law, and reused for the divergence formula.

concepts.name: proper volume element
concepts.definition: The physically measured four-volume of a small coordinate cell, equal to (-g)^{1/2} d^4x in arbitrary coordinates (g^{1/2} d^n x for a positive-definite metric).
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from the local inertial frame, where d^4x is the rods-and-clocks volume, then carried to any coordinates with the determinant identity; checked against r^2 sin theta dr dtheta dphi.
concepts.notes: Flagged by the authors as the first instance of the local-flat-to-general argument.

concepts.name: covariant derivative on a curved manifold
concepts.definition: The derivative of tensor fields defined so that at any point it equals the ordinary partial derivative of components in a local inertial frame there; in general coordinates it adds one Christoffel-symbol term per index (plus for upper, minus for lower) and produces a tensor with one more lower index.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the ambiguity of comparing vectors at separate points in curved space; settled by declaring local-inertial basis vectors to have zero derivative at P, presented as a definition justified by the physics of free fall.
concepts.notes: This implicitly selects the Levi-Civita connection; the name is not used.

concepts.name: metric compatibility
concepts.definition: The covariant derivative of the metric (and of its inverse) is zero in every basis, so raising and lowering indices commutes with covariant differentiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown at P in a local inertial frame, where it reduces to vanishing first derivatives of g, and promoted as a tensor equation; the inverse-metric version is used for the contracted Bianchi identities.
prerequisites: covariant derivative on a curved manifold

concepts.name: symmetry of Christoffel symbols
concepts.definition: Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} = Gamma^mu_{beta alpha} in any coordinate basis; geometrically the connection has no torsion.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed to obtain the metric formula for Gamma; proof deferred to Exercise 6.5 via the local inertial frame.
prerequisites: covariant derivative on a curved manifold
concepts.notes: 'Torsion' is not named.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols from the metric
concepts.definition: The connection coefficients are half the inverse metric contracted with a symmetric-minus combination of first metric derivatives (Eq. 6.32, see formulas). A clever coordinate choice can make them vanish at one point, but not their derivatives, which contain second derivatives of g.
concepts.how_introduced: Recovered from metric compatibility plus symmetry exactly as in the flat-plane work of Chapter 5, now valid for any metric.
concepts.notes: In flat space a coordinate system with Gamma = 0 everywhere exists; in curved space only at a point.

concepts.name: contracted Christoffel symbol
concepts.definition: Gamma^alpha_{mu alpha} = (1/2) g^{alpha beta} g_{alpha beta,mu} = (sqrt(-g))_{,mu}/sqrt(-g), obtained because an antisymmetric combination contracted with the symmetric inverse metric vanishes and by differentiating the determinant.
concepts.how_introduced: A shortcut prepared for the divergence formula.

concepts.name: covariant divergence formula
concepts.definition: For a vector field, V^alpha_{;alpha} = (-g)^{-1/2} partial_alpha[(-g)^{1/2} V^alpha], which avoids computing Christoffel symbols.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the contracted Christoffel identity; Exercise 6.9 checks it reproduces the polar-coordinate divergence of Chapter 5.

concepts.name: Gauss's law on a curved manifold
concepts.definition: The integral of V^alpha_{;alpha} over a four-region with the proper volume element equals the outward flux of V through its boundary computed with the proper surface element n_alpha sqrt(-g) d^3S.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows because sqrt(-g) times the covariant divergence is an ordinary coordinate divergence, to which the flat-space theorem of 4.9 applies.

concepts.name: intrinsic versus extrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: Intrinsic curvature is fixed by measurements made entirely within the manifold (distances and parallelism along paths lying in it); extrinsic curvature describes how the manifold bends inside a larger space. A cylinder is extrinsically curved but intrinsically flat; a sphere is intrinsically curved.
concepts.how_introduced: A cylinder rolled from paper keeps all distances, so a 2D ant on it finds Euclid's axioms hold; spacetime curvature in GR is declared intrinsic since world lines cannot leave spacetime, whatever higher-dimensional theories suggest.

concepts.name: Euclid's parallel postulate
concepts.definition: The axiom that two straight lines which start parallel remain parallel when extended; it holds on a plane or cylinder and fails on intrinsically curved surfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Used twice: as the test that fails on the sphere, and, once 'extended' is read as 'keeps its own direction', as the source of the definition of a geodesic.

concepts.name: failure of parallelism on a sphere
concepts.definition: On a sphere, two great circles that both cross the equator at right angles (and so start parallel) approach each other and meet at the pole, so initially parallel straight lines do not stay parallel.
concepts.how_introduced: First pictorial evidence of intrinsic curvature (Figure 6.1).

concepts.name: path dependence of parallel transport
concepts.definition: On a curved manifold the result of carrying a vector parallel to itself between two points depends on the route, and a vector taken round a closed loop generally returns rotated; hence globally parallel vector fields do not exist and vectors at different points cannot be compared absolutely.
concepts.how_introduced: Demonstrated on a sphere with a triangle having two corners on the equator and one at the pole, where the vector comes back turned by 90 degrees (Figure 6.3), contrasted with the unchanged vector on a flat loop (Figure 6.2).
concepts.notes: Exercise 6.10 generalizes: the rotation angle equals the triangle's angular excess. 'Holonomy' is not used in the book.

concepts.name: parallel transport
concepts.definition: Carrying a vector along a curve so that its covariant derivative along the curve's tangent vanishes, U^beta V^alpha_{;beta} = 0; in a local inertial frame at each point the components are momentarily constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Formalized just after the sphere construction: constant components in a local inertial frame at P give a frame-independent condition.
prerequisites: covariant derivative on a curved manifold
tangent vector as derivative along a curve
concepts.notes: Transport preserves inner products (Exercise 6.13), so a geodesic's timelike, null or spacelike character is preserved.

concepts.name: geodesic
concepts.definition: A curve whose tangent vector is parallel-transported along itself, nabla_U U = 0; in coordinates this is a second-order quasi-linear ODE for x^alpha(lambda) with a unique solution for a given starting point and initial tangent.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by asking what Euclid meant by extending a line: not keeping a constant distance from another line, but continuing in the same direction, i.e. transporting the tangent. In a local inertial frame geodesics are straight.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic in which the geodesic equation holds in the form nabla_U U = 0; any other such parameter is a linear function a lambda + b of it, and for non-null geodesics proper length (or proper time) is affine.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by substituting a linear change of parameter; a nonlinearly reparametrized copy of the same path is, strictly, not a geodesic curve.
concepts.notes: For null geodesics proper length is zero and cannot serve as the parameter; the summary in 6.7 omits this exception.

concepts.name: extremal length property of geodesics
concepts.definition: Among nearby curves with the same endpoints, a geodesic has stationary length: first-order variations do not change it, and the Euler-Lagrange equations for the length integral reproduce the geodesic equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated and strongly recommended as an exercise (Exercises 6.13-6.15).
concepts.notes: Stationary need not mean minimal; in spacetime timelike geodesics locally maximize proper time.

concepts.name: Riemann curvature tensor
concepts.definition: The (1 3) tensor with components R^alpha_{beta mu nu} = Gamma^alpha_{beta nu,mu} - Gamma^alpha_{beta mu,nu} + Gamma^alpha_{sigma mu} Gamma^sigma_{beta nu} - Gamma^alpha_{sigma nu} Gamma^sigma_{beta mu}. Given a basis one-form, a vector and the two edge vectors of a small loop, it returns the corresponding component of the change in that vector after parallel transport around the loop; it characterizes curvature completely.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed by transporting V around an infinitesimal loop of coordinate lines (Figure 6.5), integrating the transport law along each edge, expanding the pairwise differences to first order in the loop size, eliminating derivatives of V, and arguing tensor character from linearity in all four inputs.
concepts.notes: The loop formula holds only for loops small enough that second derivatives of Gamma are negligible; overall sign and index conventions vary between books (footnote 1).

concepts.name: Riemann tensor in a local inertial frame
concepts.definition: At the origin of locally inertial coordinates, where Gamma = 0, the all-lower Riemann tensor equals one half of a four-term alternating combination of second partial derivatives of the metric (Eq. 6.68, see formulas), with no first-derivative or Gamma-squared pieces.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by differentiating the Christoffel formula at P, dropping quadratic Gamma terms and using symmetric partial derivatives.
concepts.notes: Not a tensor equation: valid only at that point in that frame.

concepts.name: symmetries of the Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: With all indices lowered, R_{alpha beta mu nu} changes sign when the first two or the last two indices are swapped and is unchanged when the two pairs are exchanged; these hold in every basis.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the local-inertial-frame expression and promoted as tensor equations.
prerequisites: Riemann tensor in a local inertial frame

concepts.name: cyclic identity
concepts.definition: Holding the first index of the all-lower Riemann tensor fixed and cycling the remaining three through their cyclic permutations, the three resulting components add up to zero (Eq. 6.70).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed with the pair symmetries (Eq. 6.70); in four dimensions it removes one further component.
concepts.notes: Schutz reserves the name 'Bianchi identities' for the differential identities of 6.6.

concepts.name: number of independent Riemann components
concepts.definition: In n dimensions the Riemann tensor has n^2(n^2-1)/12 independent components: 20 in four dimensions (256 reduced to 21 by the pair symmetries and to 20 by the cyclic identity), 6 in three and 1 in two.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated for four dimensions with the reduction set as Exercise 6.18, and matched with the 20 irreducible second derivatives of the counting proof; Exercise 6.29 uses the 2D count for the sphere.
prerequisites: curvature as irreducible second derivatives of the metric
concepts.notes: The general-n formula is standard but not written in the chapter.

concepts.name: flatness criterion
concepts.definition: A manifold is flat, meaning parallel transport is path independent and a vector can be carried around any closed curve unchanged, exactly when its Riemann tensor vanishes everywhere.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted from the loop definition; the converse direction rests on the integrability condition of Exercise 6.11, and the polar-coordinate plane is suggested as a check (Exercise 6.19).

concepts.name: commutator of covariant derivatives
concepts.definition: Second covariant derivatives do not commute in curved space: [nabla_alpha, nabla_beta] V^mu = R^mu_{nu alpha beta} V^nu, and for a higher-rank tensor there is one Riemann term for each index.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed at P in locally inertial coordinates, where Gamma vanishes but its derivatives do not, then compared with the Riemann definition; interpreted as the infinitesimal analogue of stepping round a loop in two different orders.
prerequisites: covariant derivative on a curved manifold
concepts.notes: The name 'Ricci identity' is not used. For lower indices the book's all-plus form writes the lowered index first on R, which equals minus the more common R^sigma_{nu alpha beta} arrangement.

concepts.name: connecting vector
concepts.definition: A small vector that reaches from a point on one geodesic to the point with the same affine-parameter value on a neighbouring geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined with Figure 6.6 as the variable whose evolution measures relative acceleration of the geodesics.

concepts.name: geodesic deviation
concepts.definition: For neighbouring geodesics with tangent V and connecting vector xi, the relative acceleration is nabla_V nabla_V xi^alpha = R^alpha_{mu nu beta} V^mu V^nu xi^beta; initially parallel geodesics keep a constant separation only where this curvature term vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by writing the geodesic equation at two nearby points in a local inertial frame centred on one, Taylor-expanding Gamma to the other, and converting the coordinate second derivative of xi into a second covariant derivative using initial parallelism.

concepts.name: tidal forces as spacetime curvature
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration of nearby freely falling particles, the part of a gravitational field that cannot be removed by falling freely, is represented geometrically by the Riemann tensor via geodesic deviation.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in one sentence as the physical reading of Eq. 6.87; detailed use is left to later chapters.

concepts.name: Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: Keep the first index pair of the covariant derivative of the all-lower Riemann tensor fixed and cycle the derivative index together with the last two indices; the three terms always sum to zero, for every metric (Eq. 6.90).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by differentiating the local-inertial-frame form of Riemann, using the symmetry of third partial derivatives and of the metric, then replacing commas by semicolons because Gamma = 0 at the point.
prerequisites: Riemann tensor in a local inertial frame

concepts.name: Ricci tensor
concepts.definition: The (0 2) tensor R_{alpha beta} = R^mu_{alpha mu beta}, the contraction of the Riemann tensor on its first and third indices; it is symmetric, and every other contraction of Riemann is zero or plus/minus this one.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined when needed to contract the Bianchi identities; uniqueness and symmetry are set as Exercise 6.25.
concepts.notes: Some authors contract different slots, which can flip the sign; check before mixing sources.

concepts.name: Ricci scalar
concepts.definition: The scalar R = g^{mu nu} R_{mu nu}, the full trace of the Ricci tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined immediately after the Ricci tensor.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: One trace of the Bianchi identities relates derivatives of the Ricci tensor to the divergence of Riemann (Eq. 6.93); a second trace shows that twice the mixed Ricci tensor minus the Kronecker delta times the Ricci scalar has vanishing divergence (Eq. 6.97).
concepts.how_introduced: Successive contractions with the inverse metric, which passes through covariant derivatives by metric compatibility, with antisymmetry of Riemann used to fix signs.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor G^{alpha beta} = R^{alpha beta} - (1/2) g^{alpha beta} R, built from curvature and the metric, whose divergence vanishes identically; its ten independent components obey four differential identities.
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges as the natural combination in the twice-contracted Bianchi identities; Einstein's recognition of its importance and the equation G = 8 pi T are previewed.

concepts.name: local energy-momentum conservation from geometry
concepts.definition: If the field equations equate G^{alpha beta} with 8 pi T^{alpha beta}, the identity G^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0 forces T^{alpha beta}_{;beta} = 0, so local conservation of energy and momentum is guaranteed by geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: A brief parenthetical look ahead to Chapter 8.

concepts.name: integrability condition for parallel fields
aliases: condition for a globally parallel vector field
concepts.definition: The equations V^alpha_{;beta} = 0 can be solved on a region only if (Gamma^alpha_{mu beta,nu} - Gamma^alpha_{mu nu,beta} + Gamma^alpha_{sigma nu} Gamma^sigma_{mu beta} - Gamma^alpha_{sigma beta} Gamma^sigma_{mu nu}) V^mu = 0, i.e. the Riemann tensor contracted with V vanishes; the condition is also sufficient.
concepts.how_introduced: Developed in Exercise 6.11 from equality of mixed partial derivatives of V.

concepts.name: angular excess
concepts.definition: For a triangle bounded by great-circle arcs on a sphere, the amount by which its interior angles sum to more than 180 degrees; it equals the rotation of a vector transported around the triangle.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as Exercise 6.10, generalizing the octant example.
concepts.notes: The excess also equals the enclosed area divided by r^2 (Girard's theorem), a fact not stated in the book.

concepts.name: Lie bracket and Lie derivative
concepts.definition: The vector field obtained by differentiating V along U and subtracting the derivative of U along V (Eq. 6.100). The Christoffel terms cancel, so ordinary partial derivatives suffice. It satisfies a product rule and therefore serves as a derivative of V along U, the Lie derivative, requiring no metric or connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 6.39, which extends the derivative to one-forms.
prerequisites: covariant derivative on a curved manifold

concepts.name: Riemann sign and index conventions
concepts.definition: Textbooks disagree on the overall sign of the Riemann tensor and on which index positions play which role, so formulas must be checked against each author's definition; Schutz's Eq. 6.63 and Ricci contraction on first and third indices agree with Misner, Thorne and Wheeler.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised in a footnote to the definition of the Riemann tensor (recovered from the page render; dropped from the text export).
concepts.notes: The agreement with MTW is our observation, not a statement in the book.

key_equations.name: Tangent vector acting on a gradient
key_equations.meaning: The tangent to a curve is the linear machine that turns the gradient of any scalar into that scalar's rate of change along the curve; no metric is needed.
key_equations.symbols: V tangent vector; lambda curve parameter; phi scalar field; d-tilde phi its gradient one-form

key_equations.name: Canonical metric at a point
key_equations.meaning: At any single point a basis change can bring a metric with one negative and three positive eigenvalues to the Minkowski form; its trace, +2, is the signature.
key_equations.symbols: Lambda^{alpha'}_beta pointwise basis change; eta Minkowski metric

key_equations.name: Local flatness
key_equations.meaning: In suitable coordinates centred on P the metric differs from Minkowski only at second order in coordinate distance. The book prints the order symbol as a zero, '0[...]'.
key_equations.symbols: x^mu coordinates with origin at P

key_equations.name: Metric equals eta at P
key_equations.meaning: Zeroth-order local-flatness condition, achievable at any point.
key_equations.symbols: P the chosen point

key_equations.name: First derivatives vanish at P
key_equations.meaning: First-order local-flatness condition; together with 6.4 it implies Gamma = 0 at P, so free particles move on locally straight lines there.

key_equations.name: Second derivatives survive
key_equations.meaning: Some second derivatives cannot be removed unless the manifold is flat; they encode curvature.

key_equations.name: Length of a curve
key_equations.meaning: Length as the accumulated square root of the absolute value of the line element; the absolute value lets the same formula serve spacelike and timelike curves.

key_equations.name: Length of a curve in components
key_equations.meaning: Integrating the square root of the absolute line element along a parametrized curve gives its length.
key_equations.symbols: lambda_0, lambda_1 endpoint parameters

key_equations.name: Proper length
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate-free length of an arbitrary curve in terms of its tangent vector.
key_equations.symbols: V = dx/d lambda

key_equations.name: Volume element and Jacobian
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate volume elements are related by the determinant of the transformation matrix.
key_equations.symbols: unprimed: local inertial coordinates at P; primed: arbitrary coordinates

key_equations.name: Metric transformation as matrices
key_equations.meaning: The transformation law for metric components written as a matrix product, the step that makes determinants easy.
key_equations.symbols: (g) matrix of g_{alpha' beta'}; T transpose

key_equations.name: Determinant of the metric
key_equations.meaning: Because det eta = -1 and det Lambda = det Lambda^T, the metric determinant is minus the squared Jacobian, hence negative.

key_equations.name: Jacobian from the metric
key_equations.meaning: The Jacobian from local inertial to arbitrary coordinates is the square root of minus the metric determinant.
key_equations.symbols: g metric determinant in primed coordinates

key_equations.name: Proper volume element
key_equations.meaning: The physically measured four-volume in arbitrary coordinates; prototype of generalizing a flat-space notion through local inertial frames.

key_equations.name: Spherical-coordinate check
key_equations.meaning: For a positive-definite 3D metric the proper volume is sqrt(g) d^3x; in spherical polars this yields the familiar volume element.
key_equations.symbols: r, theta, phi spherical coordinates

key_equations.name: Taylor expansion of the transformation matrix
key_equations.latex: \Lambda^{\alpha}{}_{\mu'}(\vec x) = \Lambda^{\alpha}{}_{\mu'}\big|_{\mathcal P} + (x^{\gamma'}-x_0^{\gamma'})\frac{\partial^2x^{\alpha}}{\partial x^{\gamma'}\partial x^{\mu'}}\Big|_{\mathcal P} + \tfrac12(x^{\gamma'}-x_0^{\gamma'})(x^{\lambda'}-x_0^{\lambda'})\frac{\partial^3x^{\alpha}}{\partial x^{\lambda'}\partial x^{\gamma'}\partial x^{\mu'}}\Big|_{\mathcal P} + \cdots
key_equations.meaning: The unknown coordinate change is specified by its derivatives at P, which are the free parameters counted in the proof.
key_equations.symbols: x_0^{gamma'} coordinates of P

key_equations.name: Transformation law used in the proof
key_equations.meaning: Metric components in the new coordinates in terms of the old ones.

key_equations.name: Expanded metric in the new coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Order by order, the new metric's value and derivatives at P depend linearly on the coordinate-change derivatives, which sets up the counting.

key_equations.name: Ten conditions for g = eta
key_equations.meaning: Ten symmetric equations for sixteen unknowns; six unknowns remain, matching boosts and rotations.

key_equations.name: Forty conditions for vanishing first derivatives
key_equations.meaning: Exactly matched by the forty second derivatives of the coordinate change, so there is a unique solution given Lambda at P.

key_equations.name: Counting summary
key_equations.meaning: Surplus or deficit of free coordinate-change parameters at zeroth, first and second order; the 20 second derivatives that remain are the curvature.
key_equations.symbols: numbers for n = 4; three symmetric indices give n(n+1)(n+2)/3! = 20 combinations

key_equations.name: Covariant equals partial at P
key_equations.latex: V^{\alpha}{}_{;\beta} = V^{\alpha}{}_{,\beta}\quad \text{at } \mathcal P \text{ in a local inertial frame}
key_equations.meaning: The definition of the covariant derivative: in locally inertial coordinates at P the Christoffel terms are absent.

key_equations.name: Metric compatibility
key_equations.meaning: The metric is covariantly constant everywhere, established in a local inertial frame and promoted as a tensor equation.

key_equations.name: Christoffel symbols from the metric
key_equations.meaning: The connection is fixed by first derivatives of the metric; valid for any metric once Gamma is known to be symmetric (Exercise 6.5).

key_equations.name: Covariant derivatives of vectors, one-forms and (2 0) tensors
key_equations.latex: V^{\alpha}{}_{;\beta} = V^{\alpha}{}_{,\beta} + \Gamma^{\alpha}{}_{\mu\beta}V^{\mu},\qquad p_{\alpha;\beta} = p_{\alpha,\beta} - \Gamma^{\mu}{}_{\alpha\beta}p_{\mu},\qquad T^{\alpha\beta}{}_{;\gamma} = T^{\alpha\beta}{}_{,\gamma} + \Gamma^{\alpha}{}_{\mu\gamma}T^{\mu\beta} + \Gamma^{\beta}{}_{\mu\gamma}T^{\alpha\mu}
key_equations.meaning: Working formulas: one Christoffel term per index, plus for upper and minus for lower indices.
key_equations.symbols: p_alpha one-form components; T^{alpha beta} a (2 0) tensor

key_equations.name: Divergence of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for the divergence formula: only the traced Christoffel symbol enters, which is why a determinant shortcut is possible.

key_equations.name: Contracted Christoffel symbol
key_equations.meaning: The first bracket is antisymmetric in alpha and beta but contracted with symmetric g^{alpha beta}, so it drops out.

key_equations.name: Derivative of the metric determinant
key_equations.meaning: Standard matrix identity relating the derivative of a determinant to the inverse matrix (Exercise 6.7).

key_equations.name: Contracted Christoffel as logarithmic derivative
key_equations.meaning: Trace of the connection equals the gradient of ln sqrt(-g).

key_equations.name: Covariant divergence
key_equations.meaning: The divergence of a vector needs only the metric determinant, not individual Christoffel symbols.
Weighting the covariant divergence with the proper volume element turns the integrand into a plain coordinate divergence.

key_equations.name: Flat Gauss theorem applied to sqrt(-g) V
key_equations.meaning: Since the integrand is an ordinary coordinate divergence, the SR divergence theorem applies unchanged. (The text export shows a semicolon on the left; the printed page has an ordinary comma derivative, which is what makes the flat theorem applicable.)
key_equations.symbols: n_alpha outward normal; d^3S coordinate surface element

key_equations.name: Gauss's law on a curved manifold
key_equations.meaning: Integrating the covariant divergence over proper volume gives the flux through the boundary with the proper surface element.
The naive statement of parallel transport, valid only in locally inertial coordinates at the point, before it is rewritten covariantly.

key_equations.name: Parallel transport in a local inertial frame
key_equations.meaning: Constant components along the curve at P; the last form is frame independent. (The text export shows two semicolons; the print has a comma in the middle expression.)
key_equations.symbols: U = dx/d lambda tangent to the curve

key_equations.name: Parallel transport
key_equations.meaning: Frame-invariant definition of carrying V parallel along a curve with tangent U.

key_equations.name: Geodesic condition
key_equations.latex: \vec U \text{ tangent to a geodesic} \;\Leftrightarrow\; \nabla_{\vec U}\vec U = 0
key_equations.meaning: A geodesic transports its own tangent vector: the curved-space analogue of a straight line.

key_equations.name: Geodesic condition in components
key_equations.meaning: Component form before inserting U = dx/d lambda.

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation
key_equations.meaning: Second-order quasi-linear ODE whose solution is unique once a starting point and initial tangent are given.

key_equations.name: Affine reparametrization
key_equations.meaning: With constants a and b, the geodesic equation keeps its form in the new parameter; generic nonlinear changes spoil it.
key_equations.symbols: a, b constants along the curve

key_equations.name: Transport law along x^1
key_equations.meaning: Component form of nabla_{e_1} V = 0 along an edge of the coordinate loop.

key_equations.name: Transport from A to B
key_equations.meaning: Integrating the transport law along the first edge of the loop; analogous formulas (6.55-6.57) hold for the other edges, with sign flips for the return legs.
key_equations.symbols: a, b coordinate values of corner A; delta a, delta b loop sizes

key_equations.name: Net change around the loop
key_equations.meaning: Opposite edges nearly cancel; only the variation of Gamma V across the loop survives.

key_equations.name: First-order loop change
key_equations.meaning: Differences of edge integrals become derivatives times the coordinate area of the loop.

key_equations.name: Loop change along x^1 then x^2
key_equations.meaning: After eliminating derivatives of V with the transport law, the change is a fixed linear map applied to V, antisymmetric in the two loop directions.

key_equations.name: Loop change for general coordinate directions
key_equations.meaning: Transport first by delta a along e_nu, then delta b along e_mu, then back along both. The printed step list has a misprint, writing the third leg with 'a_nu' where e_nu is meant.

key_equations.name: Riemann curvature tensor
key_equations.meaning: Components of the (1 3) tensor giving the change of a vector transported around an infinitesimal loop; the complete local measure of curvature.
key_equations.symbols: alpha: component of the change; beta: transported vector; mu, nu: loop directions (first nu, then mu)

key_equations.meaning: In a local inertial frame first derivatives of g vanish at P, so differentiating 6.32 leaves only second metric derivatives.
